summary: Obstructive diseases make it hard to get air out: asthma, bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis, and emphysema. Boards ask you to match each one to its mechanism and histology, read spirometry and DLCO, and use the blood gas to judge how sick an asthmatic really is.

points: Atopic asthma is a type I hypersensitivity driven by Th2 cells.
IL-4 switches B cells to IgE, IL-5 recruits and activates eosinophils, IL-13 drives mucus production.
Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, releasing histamine and leukotrienes within minutes (early phase); eosinophils and Th2 cells sustain a late phase hours later.
Nonatopic triggers: viral infection, cold air, exercise, irritants, and aspirin.
Aspirin-exacerbated disease: blocking COX shunts arachidonic acid toward leukotrienes; often comes with nasal polyps.
Airway remodeling: goblet cell hyperplasia, thickened subepithelial basement membrane, submucosal gland enlargement, and smooth muscle hypertrophy.
Sputum: Curschmann spirals (coiled mucus casts with shed epithelium) and Charcot-Leyden crystals (from eosinophil protein).
notes.why: Dendritic cells present inhaled allergen to naive T cells, and IL-4 pushes them toward the Th2 lineage. Each Th2 cytokine then builds one feature of the disease: IgE arms mast cells for the fast early phase, IL-5 brings in eosinophils whose major basic protein injures epithelium in the late phase, and IL-13 drives goblet cell mucus. Repeated cycles of injury and repair remodel the airway, which is why long-standing asthma can lose part of its reversibility. In aspirin-exacerbated disease, COX inhibition removes protective PGE2 and diverts arachidonic acid down the 5-lipoxygenase path to cysteinyl leukotrienes, which constrict bronchi.

points: Wheezing, prolonged expiration, tachypnea, use of accessory muscles.
Pulsus paradoxus: systolic pressure falls more than 10 mmHg on inspiration in a severe attack.
Obstruction is reversible: FEV1 rises after a bronchodilator.
Early gas: low PaCO2 and respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, with hypoxemia from V/Q mismatch.
A normal or rising PaCO2 during an attack means the patient is tiring and nearing respiratory failure.
notes.why: Narrowed airways close earlier during expiration, so air is trapped and the lung hyperinflates, forcing the patient to breathe at high lung volume with accessory muscles. Large negative swings in intrathoracic pressure during inspiration increase right ventricular filling, push the septum toward the left ventricle, and lower left ventricular stroke volume, which produces pulsus paradoxus. Hypoxemia from V/Q mismatch drives hyperventilation that lowers PaCO2, so a PaCO2 that climbs back to normal means alveolar ventilation is failing as the respiratory muscles tire.

points: Permanent dilation of bronchi from obstruction plus necrotizing infection that destroys muscle and elastic tissue.
Causes: cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, tumor or foreign body, severe past pneumonia.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener when with situs inversus): dynein arm defect, sinusitis, infertility.
Daily cough with large amounts of foul purulent sputum, hemoptysis, clubbing.
Chronic infection can cause secondary (AA) amyloidosis.
notes.why: Bronchiectasis is a vicious cycle: anything that impairs clearance (thick CF mucus, immotile cilia, a blocked bronchus) lets bacteria colonize, and neutrophil elastase and other proteases digest the muscle and elastic tissue of the bronchial wall. The weakened wall dilates, pools more secretions, and invites more infection. In primary ciliary dyskinesia, absent dynein arms stop ciliary beating in airways and sinuses, immobilize sperm flagella, and, because embryonic nodal cilia set left-right asymmetry, leave organ position to chance, so about half of patients have situs inversus. Persistent inflammation keeps hepatic serum amyloid A production high, and its fragments deposit as AA amyloid.

points: Clinical definition: productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
Smoking causes mucous gland hyperplasia in the large bronchi and goblet cell metaplasia in small airways.
Reid index (gland layer thickness divided by wall thickness from epithelium to cartilage) above 0.5; normal is below about 0.4.
Blue bloater: early hypoxemia and hypercapnia, cyanosis, hypoxic vasoconstriction, then pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
notes.why: Smoke irritates the large airways, so the submucosal glands enlarge and ciliary clearance worsens; excess mucus that cannot be cleared produces the chronic productive cough that defines the disease, and the Reid index measures that gland enlargement directly. Airflow obstruction comes mainly from small airway disease: mucus plugging, goblet cell metaplasia, inflammation, and peribronchiolar fibrosis. Poorly ventilated but still perfused alveoli create low V/Q units, so hypoxemia and hypercapnia appear early, and chronic alveolar hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles until pulmonary hypertension makes the right ventricle hypertrophy and fail.

points: Destruction of alveolar walls distal to the terminal bronchiole without significant fibrosis.
Protease and antiprotease imbalance: smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages that release elastase, and oxidants inactivate alpha-1 antitrypsin.
Centriacinar: respiratory bronchioles destroyed, distal alveoli spared, upper lobes, smokers.
Panacinar: whole acinus, lower lobes, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (may also cause liver cirrhosis).
Paraseptal: distal acinus next to pleura and septa; subpleural bullae can rupture, causing spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults.
Lost elastic recoil lets small airways collapse on expiration, causing air trapping and a barrel chest.
Pink puffer: thin, dyspneic, breathes through pursed lips to keep airways open.
notes.why: Alpha-1 antitrypsin, made in the liver, normally neutralizes neutrophil elastase in the lung; emphysema develops when elastase activity outruns this protection, from extra protease (smoking) or too little inhibitor (deficiency). Smoke concentrates injury on respiratory bronchioles, giving the centriacinar pattern, while a deficient inhibitor leaves the whole acinus exposed, giving the panacinar pattern. In the PiZZ variant the misfolded protein polymerizes in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum (PAS-positive globules), which injures the liver while low serum levels expose the lung. Alveolar walls normally tether small airways open, so their loss both reduces elastic recoil and lets airways collapse in expiration, trapping air.

points: Obstruction: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 after a bronchodilator.
Air trapping raises TLC, residual volume, and FRC.
Emphysema: low DLCO because alveolar surface and capillaries are lost; gases near normal until late.
Chronic bronchitis: normal DLCO; early hypoxemia and hypercapnia from V/Q mismatch.
notes.why: FEV1 falls more than FVC when airways narrow or collapse, so the ratio drops below 0.7, and persistence after a bronchodilator separates COPD from the reversible obstruction of asthma. Air that cannot leave raises residual volume and FRC, and loss of elastic recoil lets TLC rise as well. DLCO reflects the alveolar surface area and capillary blood volume available for gas transfer, so it falls in emphysema, where alveolar walls and their capillaries are destroyed, but stays normal in chronic bronchitis, where the membrane is intact and the problem is V/Q mismatch in the airways.

tricks.text: A breathless asthmatic should be blowing off CO2. If the PaCO2 is normal or climbing, the breathing muscles are failing, which is an emergency.

tricks.text: Chronic bronchitis wrecks V/Q matching early, so the patient is cyanotic and retains CO2. Emphysema loses alveoli and capillaries together, so matching is kept and the patient works hard to stay pink.

tricks.text: Panacinar, lower lobe emphysema in a young person, especially a nonsmoker, points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Check the liver for cirrhosis from the misfolded protein.

Centriacinar emphysema is upper lobe and smoking; panacinar is lower lobe and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
Paraseptal emphysema bullae cause spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults.
COPD: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with increased TLC and residual volume.
DLCO is low in emphysema and normal in chronic bronchitis and asthma.
Bronchiectasis plus situs inversus and infertility suggests Kartagener syndrome.
Aspirin-exacerbated asthma comes with nasal polyps and leukotriene excess.
pitfalls: Asthma and COPD both lower FEV1/FVC; reversibility with a bronchodilator favors asthma.
A normal PaCO2 in an acute asthma attack is a warning sign and should not be read as reassurance.
Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation; chronic bronchitis has normal sized airways with excess mucus glands.
Air trapping raises TLC in obstructive disease; restrictive disease lowers TLC.

summary: Upper respiratory infections and inflammation run from the nose to the large bronchi. Boards ask you to tell the croup child from the epiglottitis child, strep throat from mono, and allergic from infectious rhinitis, and to predict the dangerous complications of sinusitis and strep pharyngitis.

points: Acute bronchitis: mostly viral, self-limited inflammation of the trachea and large bronchi.
Cough lasts up to about 3 weeks; chest radiograph shows no consolidation, which separates it from pneumonia.
Chronic bronchitis needs a productive cough for 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
Acute laryngitis: usually viral or from voice overuse; hoarseness without stridor or a toxic child.
notes.why: Respiratory viruses infect and shed the ciliated epithelium of the trachea and bronchi, and the exposed, inflamed mucosa keeps cough receptors sensitized until the epithelium regrows, which is why the cough can outlast the fever by weeks. Because the infection stays in the conducting airways and does not fill alveoli, there is no consolidation on the radiograph and gas exchange is preserved. Laryngitis follows the same logic at the vocal folds: mucosal edema changes how the folds vibrate and causes hoarseness, but in the wide adult larynx the swelling rarely narrows the airway enough to cause stridor.

points: Croup: parainfluenza virus laryngotracheobronchitis, 6 months to 3 years old, barking cough, inspiratory stridor.
Croup film: steeple sign (subglottic narrowing) on a frontal neck radiograph.
Epiglottitis: classically Haemophilus influenzae type b in unvaccinated children; sudden high fever, drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod posture.
Epiglottitis film: thumb sign (swollen epiglottis) on lateral neck radiograph; the airway can close suddenly, so do not agitate the child or probe the throat.
Bacterial tracheitis: toxic child with high fever and thick purulent tracheal secretions, often Staphylococcus aureus, often after a viral illness.
notes.why: Stridor is turbulent flow through a narrowed upper airway, and in a child small amounts of edema matter because resistance rises with the fourth power of a falling radius (Poiseuille law). In croup, parainfluenza inflames the subglottis, which is ringed by the complete cricoid cartilage and cannot expand outward, so edema narrows the lumen inward and creates the steeple sign. Epiglottitis is a bacterial cellulitis of the supraglottic tissues, and the swollen epiglottis can fall over the glottis, which is why agitation or a tongue blade can trigger complete obstruction. Hib vaccine targets the polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule, the main virulence factor, so epiglottitis is now rare in vaccinated children.

points: Allergic rhinitis: type I hypersensitivity; IgE on mast cells, eosinophils in nasal secretions.
Pale, boggy, bluish turbinates, sneezing, itching, clear rhinorrhea; seasonal (pollens) or perennial (dust mites, animal dander).
Common cold: rhinovirus, a nonenveloped positive-sense RNA picornavirus.
Rhinovirus is acid labile, so it does not survive the stomach, and grows best near 33 °C (91.4 °F) in the cool nose; the major group binds ICAM-1.
Vasomotor rhinitis: nonallergic, triggered by temperature change, odors, or spicy food; no IgE or eosinophils.
notes.why: In allergic rhinitis, allergen cross-links IgE on nasal mast cells, and histamine stimulates sensory nerves (itch and sneezing) and makes venules leak (clear rhinorrhea and swollen turbinates). Rhinovirus biology explains where it causes disease: it replicates best near 33 °C (91.4 °F), which keeps it in the cool nasal passages, and its acid lability means it is not a gut pathogen, unlike the related acid-stable enteroviruses. Vasomotor rhinitis is thought to reflect autonomic imbalance with parasympathetic dominance, causing glandular secretion and vascular engorgement without immune sensitization, which is why IgE and eosinophils are absent.

points: Mucosal swelling blocks the sinus ostium, trapping secretions; most cases follow a viral cold.
Bacterial causes: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (nontypeable), Moraxella catarrhalis.
Orbital cellulitis: ethmoid infection spreads through the thin lamina papyracea; proptosis, painful eye movement.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis: ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI), V1 and V2 numbness, headache, fever.
Mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis: Rhizopus or Mucor invade vessels, black necrotic tissue on palate or turbinates.
notes.why: Sinuses stay healthy only while mucociliary clearance moves secretions out through narrow ostia; viral mucosal swelling closes those ostia, and trapped, poorly oxygenated secretions favor overgrowth of the same bacteria that colonize the nasopharynx. Complications follow the anatomy: the paper-thin lamina papyracea separates the ethmoid air cells from the orbit, and valveless ophthalmic and facial veins carry infection back to the cavernous sinus, where CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI run in or along its walls. Mucor and Rhizopus thrive in ketoacidosis because acidosis impairs neutrophil function and frees iron from transferrin, and their hyphae invade arteries, causing ischemic black necrosis.

points: Streptococcus pyogenes: beta-hemolytic, bacitracin sensitive, group A; M protein resists phagocytosis.
Strep throat: fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, no cough.
Viral pharyngitis: cough, runny nose, hoarseness, conjunctivitis.
Rheumatic fever about 2 to 4 weeks after strep pharyngitis only: antibodies to M protein cross-react with heart proteins (molecular mimicry).
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows throat or skin infection: immune complex deposition, hematuria, edema, hypertension.
Mono (EBV infects B cells via CD21): exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly, fatigue.
Mono blood: atypical lymphocytes (reactive CD8 T cells) and heterophile antibodies (Monospot).
Peritonsillar abscess: severe one-sided throat pain, trismus, muffled hot potato voice, uvula pushed to the opposite side.
notes.why: Group A streptococcus causes disease both by direct infection and by immune cross-reaction. M protein interferes with complement deposition and phagocytosis, making it the main virulence factor, but antibodies raised against it can cross-react with cardiac myosin and other heart proteins, producing rheumatic fever only after pharyngitis. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis works differently: nephritogenic strains from throat or skin form immune complexes that deposit in glomeruli and activate complement, which is why serum C3 is low. EBV enters B cells through CD21 (complement receptor 2), and the large CD8 T cell response against infected B cells produces the atypical lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.

Parainfluenza virus is the main cause of croup.

Mucormycosis of the sinuses is a classic complication of diabetic ketoacidosis.

Bacterial tracheitis can look like severe croup, but the child is toxic and has thick pus in the trachea.
Pale boggy mucosa with eosinophils is allergic; a red swollen mucosa with neutrophils fits infection.

summary: The pleural space can fill with air, blood, lymph, or fluid, and the lung can collapse from blockage or compression. Boards ask you to name the fluid from its lab values, predict which way the trachea moves, and recognize asbestos and chest trauma patterns.

points: Light criteria: exudate if pleural to serum protein above 0.5, pleural to serum LDH above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two thirds of the serum upper limit.
Transudate (low protein, from pressure changes): heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome.
Exudate (leaky inflamed pleura): pneumonia, malignancy, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis, autoimmune disease.
Chylothorax: thoracic duct disruption by trauma, surgery, or lymphoma; milky fluid, triglycerides above 110 mg/dL, chylomicrons.
Hemothorax: pleural fluid hematocrit at least half the blood hematocrit; from trauma, vessel rupture, or tumor.
Large hemothorax can cause hypovolemic shock; undrained clot organizes into fibrothorax that traps the lung.
Empyema: pus in the pleural space, usually after pneumonia.
notes.why: Pleural fluid normally forms from parietal pleural capillaries and drains through parietal lymphatics, so fluid builds up when Starling forces shift or when inflammation makes capillaries leak protein. Transudates come from raised hydrostatic pressure (heart failure) or reduced oncotic pressure (cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome) across an intact membrane, so little protein or LDH enters; exudates come from inflamed or invaded pleura that lets protein and cells through. Light criteria compare pleural with serum values because a leaky membrane raises pleural protein, and pleural LDH reflects local inflammation and cell turnover. Chylothorax is milky because the thoracic duct carries chylomicrons absorbed from the gut.

points: Obstructive (resorption): a mucus plug, tumor, or foreign body blocks a bronchus and trapped air is absorbed into blood.
Resorption collapse pulls the mediastinum and trachea toward the collapsed side.
Compression atelectasis: fluid, air, or tumor pushes on the lung; mediastinum shifts away.
Contraction atelectasis: fibrosis prevents full expansion and is not reversible.
notes.why: When a bronchus is blocked, the air beyond it is trapped, and because mixed venous blood has a lower total gas pressure than air, the alveolar gas diffuses into the blood until the segment collapses. The lost volume pulls the trachea and mediastinum toward the collapsed side. Compression atelectasis works the other way: fluid, air, or tumor adds volume to that hemithorax and pushes the mediastinum away. Contraction atelectasis is not reversible because fibrous scar, not air or fluid, limits expansion.

points: Exam: hyperresonance, absent or reduced breath sounds, reduced fremitus on the affected side.
Primary spontaneous: tall thin young men (often smokers) with ruptured apical subpleural blebs.
Secondary: underlying lung disease such as COPD or cystic fibrosis.
Tension: a one-way valve lets air in but not out; trachea shifts away, venous return falls, neck veins distend, blood pressure drops.
notes.why: Intrapleural pressure is normally negative because the lung's elastic recoil pulls inward while the chest wall springs outward. Once air enters the space the two separate: the lung collapses toward the hilum and the chest wall on that side springs slightly outward. Air between lung and chest wall transmits sound and vibration poorly, which explains reduced breath sounds and fremitus with hyperresonant percussion. In tension pneumothorax, pressure becomes positive and rises with each breath, compressing the great veins and shifting the mediastinum, so venous return and cardiac output fall and obstructive shock follows.

points: Pleural plaques: well-circumscribed, often calcified plaques on the parietal pleura and diaphragm; the most common asbestos lesion.
Also benign pleural effusion and diffuse pleural fibrosis; asbestosis itself is lower lobe interstitial fibrosis.
Ferruginous bodies: golden brown beaded fibers coated with iron-containing protein (Prussian blue positive).
Bronchogenic carcinoma is the most common cancer after asbestos exposure, and risk multiplies with smoking.
Mesothelioma risk rises with asbestos but is not linked to smoking.
notes.why: Asbestos fibers, especially the straight amphiboles, are long and thin enough that macrophages cannot fully engulf them, and this frustrated phagocytosis keeps the macrophages releasing reactive oxygen species and fibrogenic cytokines. Fibers that reach the pleura drive parietal plaque formation and, over decades, mesothelial DNA damage that can lead to mesothelioma. Fibers become ferruginous bodies when macrophages coat them with iron-containing protein. Asbestos and smoking multiply each other's effect on bronchogenic carcinoma, while mesothelioma depends on the fibers alone, which is why smoking does not change its risk.

points: Mediastinitis: esophageal perforation, infection after sternotomy, or inhalational anthrax (hemorrhagic, widened mediastinum).
Pneumomediastinum: air dissects into the mediastinum; subcutaneous crepitus and a Hamman crunch heard with each heartbeat.
Costochondritis: chest wall pain with reproducible tenderness over the costochondral junctions.
notes.why: The mediastinum is a continuous connective tissue compartment, so infection or air that enters it spreads freely: esophageal rupture lets oral flora and gastric contents in, and inhaled Bacillus anthracis spores are carried by macrophages to mediastinal lymph nodes, where toxin causes hemorrhagic necrosis and a widened mediastinum. In pneumomediastinum, air from ruptured alveoli tracks along the bronchovascular sheaths to the hilum (the Macklin effect) and then into the neck and chest wall, giving crepitus; the heart beating against air-filled tissue makes the crunch. Costochondritis pain is reproducible on palpation because it comes from the chest wall itself, not the heart or pleura.

points: Flail chest: several adjacent ribs broken in two places; the segment moves inward on inspiration (paradoxical motion).
Pulmonary contusion: hemorrhage into alveoli with hypoxemia that worsens over the following hours.
Open pneumothorax: a penetrating wound lets air enter the pleural space with each breath.
Diaphragmatic rupture: more often on the left, so stomach or bowel appears in the left hemithorax.
notes.why: A flail segment is no longer attached to the rest of the rib cage, so it follows pleural pressure instead of the chest wall: it sinks inward as pleural pressure falls in inspiration and bulges outward in expiration, which reduces effective tidal volume. The underlying pulmonary contusion is often the bigger threat because blood and edema fill alveoli progressively, creating shunt and worsening hypoxemia over hours. A chest wound wider than about two thirds of the tracheal diameter offers less resistance than the airway, so air enters through the wound. The liver protects the right hemidiaphragm, which is why blunt rupture is more often recognized on the left.

charts.title: Which way does the trachea move?

tricks.label: Collapse pulls, mass pushes
tricks.text: When air leaves the lung (resorption atelectasis), the chest loses volume and the trachea is pulled toward that side. When something fills the chest (fluid, tension air), the trachea is pushed away.

tricks.label: Half the hematocrit means blood
tricks.text: Bloody looking fluid needs only a little blood. Call it a hemothorax only when the fluid hematocrit is at least half the blood hematocrit.

tricks.label: Asbestos plus smoking multiplies
tricks.text: Lung carcinoma risk from asbestos and smoking together is far higher than either alone. Mesothelioma risk does not change with smoking.

highYield: Exudate if any Light criterion is met: protein ratio above 0.5, LDH ratio above 0.6, or LDH above two thirds of the serum upper limit.
Chylothorax: milky fluid with triglycerides above 110 mg/dL from thoracic duct injury or lymphoma.
Tension pneumothorax: trachea away, hypotension, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds.
Resorption atelectasis shifts the mediastinum toward the collapse.
Calcified parietal pleural plaques are the most common sign of asbestos exposure.
Ferruginous bodies are iron-coated asbestos fibers.
Hamman crunch with subcutaneous crepitus means pneumomediastinum.
Flail chest moves paradoxically inward on inspiration.
pitfalls: Effusion and atelectasis are both dull to percussion; effusion pushes the trachea away and atelectasis pulls it toward.
Pulmonary embolism effusions are usually exudates, so do not assume all non-infectious effusions are transudates.
Pleural plaques are benign; they mark exposure and do not turn into mesothelioma.

summary: Pulmonary vascular disease covers fluid leaking into alveoli, clots and other material lodging in the pulmonary arteries, and high pressure in the pulmonary circuit. Boards ask you to use Starling forces, predict the blood gas in pulmonary embolism, tell fat, air, and amniotic emboli apart, and classify pulmonary hypertension.

points: Fluid leaves capillaries when hydrostatic pressure pushing out beats oncotic pressure pulling in, or when the capillary wall leaks.
Cardiogenic: left heart failure raises pulmonary capillary pressure; wedge pressure above 18 mmHg.
Chronic congestion leaves hemosiderin-laden macrophages (heart failure cells) in alveoli.
Noncardiogenic causes: capillary injury (ARDS), low plasma oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), lymphatic obstruction (tumor in lymphatics).
Noncardiogenic edema from capillary injury has a normal wedge pressure and protein-rich fluid.
notes.why: Net filtration depends on the balance of capillary hydrostatic pressure, plasma oncotic pressure, and capillary permeability, with lymphatics removing the normal small leak. In left heart failure, pressure backs up through the pulmonary veins and raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, which the wedge pressure estimates; fluid fills the interstitium first and then the alveoli once lymphatic capacity is exceeded. Red cells that leak into alveoli are engulfed by macrophages, which convert hemoglobin iron to hemosiderin. When the capillary wall itself is damaged, as in ARDS, protein-rich fluid floods alveoli even though wedge pressure is normal.

points: Most emboli come from deep vein thrombosis of the leg veins above the knee.
Virchow triad: stasis (immobility, surgery, long travel), endothelial injury, hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, estrogen, factor V Leiden).
Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea.
Blood gas: hypoxemia with low PaCO2 and respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation.
Widened A-a gradient from V/Q mismatch and dead space.
D-dimer is sensitive but not specific; a normal value helps rule out embolism when suspicion is low.
A saddle embolus at the pulmonary artery bifurcation causes acute right heart strain (acute cor pulmonale) and can cause sudden death.
notes.why: An embolus stops perfusion to ventilated alveoli, creating dead space, while released mediators, bronchoconstriction, and diversion of blood to unblocked lung create low V/Q units; together these widen the A-a gradient and cause hypoxemia. Hypoxemia and stimulation of lung receptors drive hyperventilation, and because CO2 is easy to blow off, PaCO2 falls into respiratory alkalosis. Sudden obstruction of a large share of the pulmonary bed raises right ventricular afterload faster than the thin-walled ventricle can adapt, so it dilates and fails. D-dimer is a fibrin breakdown product, so it rises with any clot turnover, including surgery, cancer, and pregnancy, which limits its specificity.

points: Most emboli do not infarct the lung because the bronchial arteries keep the tissue alive.
Infarction happens when a medium or small artery is blocked and bronchial flow is poor, as in left heart failure.
Wedge shaped and hemorrhagic (red), with the base on the pleura and the apex toward the hilum.
Causes hemoptysis and pleuritic pain from fibrinous pleuritis over the infarct.
notes.why: The lung has a dual blood supply: bronchial arteries from the systemic circulation nourish the airways and supporting tissue, so blocking a pulmonary artery branch alone usually does not kill lung tissue. When bronchial flow is already poor, as in left heart failure, the downstream tissue dies. The infarct is hemorrhagic because bronchial blood keeps flowing into the dead, loose tissue, and it is wedge shaped because pulmonary arteries branch outward from the hilum toward the pleura. Involvement of the overlying pleura causes fibrinous pleuritis and pleuritic pain.

points: Fat embolism: 24 to 72 hours after a long bone or pelvic fracture; hypoxemia, confusion, petechiae on chest, axillae, and conjunctivae.
Air embolism: air entering through a central venous catheter, or nitrogen bubbles forming in tissues and blood when a diver rises too fast (decompression sickness).
Amniotic fluid embolism: during labor or just after delivery; sudden dyspnea, hypotension, seizures, and DIC; fetal squamous cells found in maternal pulmonary vessels.
notes.why: Fat embolism combines mechanical and biochemical injury: marrow fat globules lodge in pulmonary and systemic microvessels, and free fatty acids released from them injure endothelium, which is why symptoms appear after a delay of 1 to 3 days. Platelets adhere to the fat globules, contributing to thrombocytopenia and the petechial rash. In decompression sickness, nitrogen dissolved in tissues under high pressure comes out of solution as bubbles when pressure falls too fast, blocking vessels and injuring tissue. Amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation triggers an anaphylactoid response, and its tissue factor content activates coagulation, producing DIC.

points: Defined by raised mean pulmonary artery pressure at rest (above about 20 mmHg by current criteria, 25 mmHg in older sources).
Group 1, pulmonary arterial hypertension: idiopathic or heritable (BMPR2 loss of function lets smooth muscle proliferate), drugs, connective tissue disease, HIV, shunts.
Group 2: left heart disease (most common cause overall).
Group 3: lung disease or hypoxia (COPD, interstitial disease, sleep apnea, altitude) through hypoxic vasoconstriction.
Group 4: chronic thromboembolic disease.
Vessels show medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, and plexiform lesions in severe arterial disease; atherosclerosis appears in large pulmonary arteries.
Right ventricle hypertrophies, then fails (cor pulmonale): raised neck veins, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema.
notes.why: Pulmonary vascular resistance is normally low because the vessels are thin-walled and compliant, so any process that narrows, obliterates, or constricts them raises the pressure the right ventricle must generate. BMPR2 normally signals through SMAD proteins to restrain smooth muscle proliferation, so loss of function lets the media thicken and plexiform lesions form. Unlike systemic arterioles, pulmonary arterioles constrict to alveolar hypoxia, which diverts blood to better ventilated lung but becomes harmful when hypoxia is widespread and chronic. The right ventricle first hypertrophies against the higher afterload, then dilates and fails, backing blood up into the systemic veins.

points: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu): autosomal dominant; telangiectasias of skin and mucosa, nosebleeds, GI bleeding.
Pulmonary AVMs shunt blood right to left past the alveoli, causing hypoxemia that oxygen corrects poorly.
Clots and bacteria bypass the lung filter: paradoxical embolic stroke and brain abscess; AVMs can also cause hemoptysis.
notes.why: In hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, mutations in TGF-beta pathway genes such as ENG (endoglin) and ACVRL1 produce fragile, direct arteriovenous connections with no capillary bed between them. In the lung, blood crossing these shunts never meets alveolar gas, so supplemental oxygen raises PaO2 only slightly, which is the hallmark of a true shunt. The pulmonary capillary bed normally traps small clots and bacteria from venous blood, so a shunt lets them pass into systemic arteries and reach the brain.

summary: This unit covers tumors from the nose to the pleura, plus esophageal cancer. Boards ask you to match each lung cancer to its location, histology, smoking link, and paraneoplastic syndrome, predict the local effects of tumor spread, and recognize the virus-linked head and neck cancers.

points: Adenocarcinoma: most common lung cancer overall and the most common in nonsmokers and women; peripheral, gland forming, mucin producing.
Adenocarcinoma in situ: lepidic growth along intact alveolar walls with no invasion (formerly bronchioloalveolar carcinoma).
Squamous cell: central, strongly tied to smoking; keratin pearls, intercellular bridges; may cavitate.
Large cell: peripheral, poorly differentiated with no glandular or squamous features; poor prognosis.
Small cell: central, almost always in smokers; small cells, scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding; chromogranin and synaptophysin positive.
Small cell spreads early, so it is usually beyond surgery at diagnosis.
Bronchial carcinoid: low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, nests of uniform cells, chromogranin positive, often a central polypoid mass in a younger patient, not tied to smoking.
Carcinoid can block a bronchus (atelectasis, recurrent pneumonia) and rarely causes carcinoid syndrome.
notes.why: Each type reflects the cell it arises from and where that cell sits. Squamous and small cell carcinomas arise centrally in bronchi heavily exposed to smoke carcinogens; squamous cell carcinoma develops through squamous metaplasia and dysplasia, while small cell carcinoma arises from neuroendocrine cells, so it carries neuroendocrine markers and dense-core granules. Adenocarcinoma arises peripherally from glandular and alveolar epithelium, which is why it can grow along alveolar walls and is the type seen in nonsmokers, often with driver mutations such as EGFR or ALK. Small cell carcinoma nearly always loses TP53 and RB1, grows fast, and spreads early, so it behaves as systemic disease.

points: Squamous cell: PTHrP causes hypercalcemia.
Small cell: ACTH (Cushing syndrome) and ADH (SIADH with hyponatremia).
Small cell: Lambert-Eaton syndrome, antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels; weakness improves with repeated effort.
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (clubbing and periosteal new bone): especially adenocarcinoma.
notes.why: Paraneoplastic syndromes come from what the tumor secretes or the antibodies it provokes, not from tumor bulk or metastasis. Squamous cells secrete PTHrP, which binds the PTH receptor in bone and kidney, raising calcium while native PTH is suppressed. Small cell carcinoma keeps neuroendocrine machinery and can secrete ACTH and ADH ectopically, and its antigens prompt antibodies against P/Q-type presynaptic calcium channels, which reduces acetylcholine release. In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, repeated effort lets calcium build up in the nerve terminal, so more acetylcholine is released and strength briefly improves.

points: Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumor: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) from sympathetic chain invasion, and C8 to T1 brachial plexus deficits.
Superior vena cava syndrome: facial swelling and plethora, distended neck and chest veins, arm edema; usually a central tumor.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion: hoarseness (the left nerve loops under the aortic arch).
Phrenic nerve invasion: paralyzed, elevated hemidiaphragm.
notes.why: Local signs follow the anatomy around the tumor. An apical tumor sits on the cervical sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion, the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8 to T1), and the subclavian vessels. Central and right-sided mediastinal masses compress the thin-walled superior vena cava, so venous blood from the head and arms backs up. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch near the left hilum, so left hilar disease causes hoarseness, and the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) passes anterior to the lung root, so invasion paralyzes the diaphragm on that side.

points: Metastases are more common than primary lung cancer; they appear as multiple well-circumscribed nodules.
Hamartoma: most common benign lung tumor; cartilage and fat, popcorn calcification on imaging.
Mesothelioma: asbestos exposure decades earlier, no link to smoking; recurrent hemorrhagic effusion, tumor encasing the lung.
Mesothelioma markers: calretinin and cytokeratin positive; long slender microvilli on electron microscopy.
Metastatic adenocarcinoma in the pleura: calretinin negative, often CEA positive, short stubby microvilli.
notes.why: The lung filters the entire cardiac output through its capillary bed, so blood-borne tumor cells from almost anywhere lodge there, which is why metastases outnumber primary tumors and appear as multiple round nodules. Pulmonary hamartoma is a benign growth of mature tissues native to the bronchus, mainly cartilage and fat, and its cartilage calcifies in a popcorn pattern. Mesothelioma and metastatic adenocarcinoma can look alike in the pleura, so the cell of origin is shown by markers: mesothelial cells express calretinin and have long slender microvilli, while glandular tumor cells express epithelial markers such as CEA and have short microvilli.

points: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma: EBV linked, more common in southern China and parts of Africa; nonkeratinizing or undifferentiated.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents with neck node metastasis or one-sided serous otitis media from eustachian tube blockage.
Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma: smoking and alcohol; glottic tumors cause early hoarseness.
Vocal fold nodules: benign, bilateral, from voice overuse.
Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis: HPV types 6 and 11, recurrent papillomas, hoarseness in children.
Nasal polyps: chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, aspirin-exacerbated disease with asthma, or cystic fibrosis in a child; cause obstruction and anosmia.
Vocal fold polyps: usually one-sided, from voice strain or smoking; cause hoarseness.
HPV 16 causes oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil and base of tongue, often in nonsmokers.
Tobacco and alcohol cause squamous carcinoma of the oral cavity and pharynx.
notes.why: In head and neck tumors, location and cause go together. EBV infects nasopharyngeal epithelium and its latent proteins drive proliferation, with genetic and dietary cofactors explaining the geographic clustering; a mass near the eustachian tube opening blocks middle ear drainage and causes a serous effusion. HPV 16 E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and Rb in tonsillar crypt epithelium, which is why these tumors arise in nonsmokers and overexpress p16. Glottic cancers cause hoarseness early because even a small lesion changes vocal fold vibration, and the glottis has few lymphatics, so nodal spread comes late.

points: Squamous cell: upper and middle third; smoking, alcohol, very hot drinks, achalasia, nitrosamines.
Adenocarcinoma: distal third; GERD leading to Barrett esophagus, obesity.
Both cause progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids) and weight loss; invasion forward can create a tracheoesophageal fistula with cough on swallowing.
notes.why: The two types arise from different epithelia under different injuries. Squamous cell carcinoma comes from the native squamous lining after chronic chemical and thermal injury from tobacco, alcohol, and very hot drinks. Adenocarcinoma follows chronic reflux, which replaces distal squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar epithelium (Barrett metaplasia) that can progress through dysplasia to cancer. Most of the esophagus has no serosa, so tumors invade neighboring structures such as the trachea early, and dysphagia progresses from solids to liquids as the lumen narrows.

summary: Congenital lung disease ranges from a single gene defect (cystic fibrosis) to errors in how the foregut, diaphragm, and lung buds form. Boards ask you to explain the CFTR chloride defect in sweat and airway, predict its many organ effects, and recognize tracheoesophageal fistula, diaphragmatic hernia, sequestration, and bronchogenic cyst in a newborn or child.

points: Autosomal recessive mutation in CFTR on chromosome 7; most common is deletion of phenylalanine 508 (F508del).
F508del misfolds the protein, which is degraded before it reaches the cell surface.
CFTR is an ATP-gated chloride channel; cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates CFTR so ATP can open it.
Sweat duct: CFTR normally reabsorbs chloride, and sodium follows; without it both stay in the sweat, so sweat is salty.
Airway: CFTR normally secretes chloride and restrains ENaC; without it chloride secretion falls and sodium absorption through ENaC rises.
Water follows the sodium out of the airway lumen, so airway surface liquid is depleted and mucus becomes thick and hard to clear.
notes.why: CFTR is an ABC transporter that works as a chloride channel: PKA phosphorylation of its regulatory domain, triggered by cAMP, allows ATP binding to open it. Chloride flows in opposite directions in different tissues: the sweat duct absorbs salt to make hypotonic sweat, so loss of CFTR leaves salt in sweat, while the airway secretes chloride to hydrate its surface, so loss of CFTR dehydrates it. Without CFTR restraint, ENaC absorbs more sodium, water follows osmotically, and the periciliary layer collapses so cilia cannot move mucus. F508del is a processing defect: the protein is made but misfolds and is destroyed by endoplasmic reticulum quality control.

points: Newborn: meconium ileus (thick meconium blocks the ileum).
Pancreatic insufficiency: steatorrhea, poor growth, deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Lungs: early Staphylococcus aureus, later mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa; bronchiectasis and clubbing.
Sinuses: chronic sinusitis and nasal polyps; nasal polyps in a child should prompt CF testing.
Most men are infertile from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.
Diagnosis: sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher.
notes.why: Nearly every organ problem in CF comes from dehydrated, thick secretions blocking a duct or lumen. Pancreatic ducts plug before birth, so enzymes cannot reach the gut, fat is not digested, and fat-soluble vitamins are lost in stool; in the fetal ileum, viscous meconium causes obstruction. In the airway, retained mucus is colonized by Staphylococcus aureus early and later by Pseudomonas, which switches to an alginate-producing mucoid biofilm that resists clearance and keeps neutrophils destroying bronchial walls. The vas deferens is thought to be blocked by thick secretions during fetal development and then degenerate, which explains congenital bilateral absence with normal sperm production in the testes.

points: The foregut fails to separate fully into trachea and esophagus.
Most common form: esophageal atresia (blind upper pouch) with a distal fistula from trachea to the lower esophagus.
Fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid, causing polyhydramnios.
Newborn drools and chokes, coughs, and turns cyanotic with the first feeds.
A nasogastric tube will not pass and coils in the upper pouch; air in the stomach shows the distal fistula.
Look for VACTERL: vertebral, anal atresia, cardiac, tracheoesophageal fistula, esophageal atresia, renal, and limb (radial) defects.
notes.why: The respiratory diverticulum forms as a ventral outgrowth of the foregut, and tracheoesophageal ridges fuse into a septum that separates the trachea in front from the esophagus behind. When this septation is incomplete or deviates, the esophagus ends blindly and its lower segment stays connected to the trachea. Because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid into the gut, fluid accumulates (polyhydramnios); after birth, feeds fill the upper pouch and spill into the larynx, while air passes through the distal fistula into the stomach. Gastric contents can also reflux up the fistula into the lungs and cause pneumonitis.

points: Pleuroperitoneal fold (membrane) fails to close, usually on the left posterolateral side (Bochdalek).
Abdominal contents enter the chest and compress the developing lung, causing pulmonary hypoplasia.
Newborn: severe respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in the chest, heart sounds shifted to the right.
notes.why: The diaphragm forms from the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the esophageal mesentery, and body wall muscle; the pleuroperitoneal membranes close the posterolateral openings, and the left side closes after the right. If the left opening is still patent when the midgut returns from the umbilical cord around week 10, bowel enters the chest. Compression during the period of bronchial branching leaves too few airways and alveoli and an abnormal pulmonary vascular bed, so the main threat is pulmonary hypoplasia with pulmonary hypertension, not the hernia itself. The abdomen is scaphoid because its contents sit in the thorax.

points: Pulmonary sequestration: nonfunctioning lung tissue with no bronchial connection, supplied by a systemic artery from the aorta.
Sequestration is usually in a lower lobe and becomes infected again and again.
Bronchogenic cyst: abnormal budding of the foregut; fluid-filled cyst lined by respiratory epithelium, usually in the mediastinum near the carina.
Bronchogenic cysts can compress an airway or become infected.
notes.why: Both lesions are abnormal foregut buds. A sequestration buds separately from the normal tracheobronchial tree, so it has no airway connection and is supplied by an anomalous systemic artery, usually from the aorta; with no bronchus to clear secretions, it fills with fluid and becomes infected repeatedly. A bronchogenic cyst comes from abnormal budding of the tracheal diverticulum or bronchial tree, so its wall resembles a bronchus, with ciliated respiratory epithelium, cartilage, and glands, and it usually sits near the carina where it can compress an airway.

summary: This unit covers infections of the lungs and airways, from common pneumonias to tuberculosis, fungi, and childhood infections like pertussis and RSV. Boards ask you to match the organism to the patient and the pattern on imaging, follow tuberculosis from primary to reactivation, and predict toxin effects and complications.

points: Lobar: consolidation of a whole lobe; Streptococcus pneumoniae most often, also Klebsiella (alcoholism, currant jelly sputum).
Lobar stages: congestion, red hepatization (red cells, neutrophils, fibrin), gray hepatization (red cells broken down), resolution.
Consolidation exam: dullness, increased tactile fremitus, egophony, bronchial breath sounds.
Bronchopneumonia: patchy, often multilobar, centered on bronchioles; Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas.
Atypical (interstitial): patchy interstitial infiltrates that look worse than the patient; dry cough, headache, myalgia.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae: no cell wall, cold agglutinins (IgM), young adults in close quarters such as dorms and barracks.
Others: Chlamydia pneumoniae, viruses, and Legionella (water aerosols, high fever, diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia).
notes.why: The pattern depends on how the organism spreads. Pneumococcus provokes an intra-alveolar exudate that carries bacteria through the pores of Kohn to neighboring alveoli until a whole lobe fills, and the stages track the inflammatory response: fluid, then red cells, neutrophils, and fibrin, then red cell breakdown, then enzymatic clearance. Consolidated lung conducts sound and vibration well, which explains dullness, increased fremitus, and bronchial breath sounds. Staphylococcus aureus and similar organisms start in bronchioles and spread patchily, while Mycoplasma, which lacks a cell wall, attaches to ciliated epithelium and inflames the interstitium, leaving alveoli fairly clear, so the film looks worse than the patient.

points: Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia: Pseudomonas, MRSA, and enteric gram-negative rods.
Chemical pneumonitis is sterile acid injury within hours of aspirating gastric contents; aspiration pneumonia is infection by oral bacteria over days in dependent segments.
Lung abscess: aspiration of oral anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus) in alcoholism, seizures, or dysphagia.
Abscess shows an air-fluid level, often in the right lung (posterior upper lobe or superior lower lobe if supine), with foul sputum; Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella also cause abscess.
notes.why: Aspiration follows gravity and anatomy: the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, so material usually goes right, and the dependent segments depend on posture (posterior upper lobe and superior lower lobe when supine, basal lower lobes when upright). Reduced consciousness or impaired swallowing removes the protective cough and gag, so oral anaerobes reach the lung, and the tissue necrosis they cause forms a cavity with an air-fluid level once it drains into a bronchus. Hospital and ventilator pathogens differ because hospitalized patients become colonized with resistant organisms and an endotracheal tube bypasses upper airway defenses.

points: Primary: Ghon focus in the lower upper lobe or upper lower lobe plus a hilar node (Ghon complex).
Th1 cells release IFN-gamma that activates macrophages; caseating granulomas wall off the bacilli, leaving latent infection.
Tuberculin skin test: type IV reaction read at 48 to 72 hours; can be positive after BCG vaccine.
IFN-gamma release assay: T cell response to antigens not in BCG, so BCG does not cause a false positive.
Reactivation: apical cavitation, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis; risk rises with HIV and immunosuppression.
Miliary spread: tiny seed-like nodules in kidneys, meninges, adrenals, and vertebrae (Pott disease).
notes.why: Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages by blocking phagolysosome fusion, partly through sulfatides, so control depends on cell-mediated immunity. Dendritic cells present antigen and IL-12 drives Th1 cells, whose IFN-gamma activates macrophages to kill bacilli and form granulomas with caseous centers, while TNF-alpha holds the granuloma together. This explains why TNF inhibitors and HIV reactivate latent infection and why the skin test is a delayed type IV reaction. Reactivation favors the apices because their high V/Q ratio gives the highest alveolar oxygen tension, which this strict aerobe prefers.

points: Endemic dimorphic fungi grow as molds in soil and yeasts (or spherules) in tissue; they infect healthy hosts.
Histoplasma: Ohio and Mississippi valleys, bird and bat droppings, tiny yeasts inside macrophages.
Blastomyces: similar region, broad-based budding yeast; spreads to skin and bone.
Coccidioides: southwestern US deserts, spherules with endospores; spreads to skin, bone, and meninges.
All three form granulomas that can mimic tuberculosis.
Pneumocystis: CD4 below 200 per microliter, bilateral ground-glass infiltrates, hypoxemia on exertion, high LDH.
Aspergillus: aspergilloma in an old cavity, angioinvasive disease in neutropenia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in asthma and cystic fibrosis.
notes.why: Dimorphism depends on temperature: these fungi grow as molds in the environment, releasing conidia (arthroconidia for Coccidioides) that are inhaled, and they convert to yeasts or spherules at body temperature in the lung. The tissue form resists clearance, so control requires Th1 immunity and granulomas as in tuberculosis, which is why the two look alike and why dissemination rises with impaired T cell function. Pneumocystis fills alveoli with foamy exudate that thickens the diffusion barrier, so oxygen saturation falls with exertion. Aspergillus disease depends on the host: colonizing an old cavity, invading vessels when neutrophils are absent, or provoking IgE and eosinophils in allergic hosts.

points: Pertussis stages: catarrhal (cold-like, most contagious), paroxysmal (coughing fits, inspiratory whoop, posttussive vomiting), convalescent.
Pertussis toxin causes marked lymphocytosis; young infants may have apnea instead of a whoop, and pneumonia.
RSV: most common cause of infant bronchiolitis and pneumonia; winter epidemics with wheezing and tachypnea; severe in prematurity, congenital heart disease, and chronic lung disease.
Diphtheria: gray adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped, bull neck nodes; grows on tellurite agar, Elek test shows toxin.
Diphtheria toxin inactivates EF-2; it causes myocarditis, heart block, and cranial and peripheral neuropathy.
notes.why: Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates the inhibitory Gi protein, so adenylate cyclase is no longer restrained and cAMP rises, and blocking Gi-coupled chemokine signaling keeps lymphocytes from leaving the blood, causing lymphocytosis. Tracheal cytotoxin damages ciliated cells, so mucus pools and triggers paroxysms of cough. Diphtheria toxin is encoded by a lysogenic phage and ADP-ribosylates EF-2, halting protein synthesis; local cell death forms the pseudomembrane, and toxin carried in the blood damages heart and nerves. RSV infects bronchiolar epithelium, and small infant bronchioles are easily blocked by necrotic debris and mucus, causing wheeze and air trapping.

points: Influenza destroys ciliated epithelium, opening the door to secondary Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia.
Avian and human influenza strains can swap gene segments (reassortment) and create novel pandemic strains.
Coronaviruses: some cause common colds; SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 cause severe pneumonia.
SARS-CoV-2 enters cells through ACE2 on airway and alveolar cells; loss of smell, diffuse alveolar damage, and thrombosis; risk rises with age and comorbidity.
Inhalational anthrax: hemorrhagic mediastinitis with a widened mediastinum.
Tularemia: rabbits and ticks. Q fever: Coxiella from farm animal birth products. Melioidosis: Burkholderia pseudomallei in Southeast Asia.
notes.why: Influenza hemagglutinin binds sialic acid to enter cells, and neuraminidase releases new virions; destruction of ciliated epithelium removes the mucociliary barrier, which is why secondary bacterial pneumonia follows. Because the genome is segmented, two strains infecting one cell can swap segments (antigenic shift) and create a strain the population has no immunity to, while point mutations cause smaller yearly changes (antigenic drift). SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binds ACE2, and host TMPRSS2 cleaves the spike to allow fusion; injury to alveolar cells and endothelium explains diffuse alveolar damage and thrombosis. Anthrax spores are carried by macrophages to mediastinal nodes, so inhalational anthrax presents as hemorrhagic mediastinitis rather than typical pneumonia.
